claims.text: LMAX, which was established to create a very high performance financial exchange, found in performance testing that the latency cost of passing data between stages through queues was in the same order of magnitude as the cost of IO operations to disk.
Queue implementations tend to have write contention on the head, tail and size variables, and even when head and tail use separate concurrency mechanisms they generally occupy the same cache line.
In Java, queues are also significant sources of garbage.
In LMAX's experiment of incrementing a 64-bit counter 500 million times, a single thread took 300 ms, a single thread taking a lock took 10,000 ms, and two threads sharing a lock took 224,000 ms.
The same increment took 5,700 ms on a single thread using CAS and 30,000 ms on two threads using CAS.
All memory for the ring buffer is pre-allocated on start up.
Each producer and consumer works from a strict sequence number, and with only one producer no locks or CAS operations are required, however complex the consumer graph.
The buffer size is a power of two so that a bit mask of size minus one can replace the costly remainder calculation on the sequence number.

A consumer that finds the cursor has advanced several steps can process up to that sequence without involving the concurrency mechanisms, so a lagging consumer quickly regains pace when producers burst ahead.
Over 25 million messages per second and latencies lower than 50 nanoseconds on processors at moderate clock rates, about 8 times the throughput of queues in the same configuration.

recall.prompt: Why does a single producer need no locks or CAS in the Disruptor?

answer.text: Producers and consumers work from strict sequence numbers, and with only one producer there is no write contention to arbitrate.

recall.prompt: How much slower was a locked counter than an unlocked one in LMAX's experiment?

answer.text: 300 ms unlocked on one thread, 10,000 ms with a lock on one thread, 224,000 ms with two threads sharing the lock.

recall.prompt: Why is the ring buffer's size a power of two?

answer.text: So a bit mask of size minus one can perform the remainder operation on the sequence number cheaply.
